title: Resilience and online safety review
credit: Lesson resource · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: free for classroom use, share and adapt with credit, no resale
definition: Resilience can mean adapting, taking a safe pause and asking for help when a task or change feels hard. Everyone has mental health. Thoughts and feelings can change. One sign cannot prove a condition.
case: An invented younger learner starts two familiar tasks in a new order. Their card model falls down. They feel cross and think they cannot do it. They would like a clear first step. Later they draft a photo of the model. A note in view shows private routine details. Another learner is in the photo and has not agreed to share it. A reply causes concern. No wording is shown. These are made-up scenes for this task.
model: The younger learner could feel cross after the model falls. They could try one smaller step and ask school staff, Can you show me the first step? A safe pause or a familiar gentle move may help. If one step does not help, they can ask for another way. Before sharing, leave out private details and ask before including someone else. Use kind words. A private setting may limit the audience, but someone may copy the post. Stop replying to a concerning message and ask a trusted adult for help to report or block it. Do not send it on.
products: A resilience plan for the invented younger learner: a feeling or challenge, one manageable step or strategy, a support type and private opener, and what to do if more help is needed.
An online-safety guide for the same invented younger learner: privacy and consent, why copies may remain, kind words, and a stop-and-tell route with adult help to report or block.

choices.B: Make a plan map and a short guide in panels.
choices.C: Write a short plan note and a guide in short text.

same_evidence: Both choices include BOTH products and meet the same checks. Choose one format, not one product. All work is for the made-up younger learner. No real younger pupil receives the guide.
help_route: Ask a trusted adult or school staff privately. A family doctor can discuss health and help find care. A suitable helpline can offer listening or advice; staff help find an age-appropriate route. Use words, a note, HELP or the usual aid. If the first adult is busy or help is not enough, ask another trusted adult. For an urgent concern get school staff at once. No service, website or number is named.
step_out: Before teaching, agree the discreet pause signal, available adult and familiar supervised quiet route. Staff acknowledge it privately. No public explanation is needed. Offer a neutral task, supported return or private catch-up. Do not send a learner away alone. Pass is not failure.
safeguarding: Any disclosure goes to the safeguarding lead through school procedure. Listen calmly, reassure, do not probe, investigate or promise secrecy. Follow the immediate school route for urgent concerns. Keep real concerns and personal details in the separate safeguarding record, not shared learning evidence. A pupil unable to identify a trusted adult is supported privately, not pressed.
privacy: Use only the invented learner in all class tasks. No personal mental-health history, worry, name, account, password, device, image or incident is requested. A learner may pass or use the agreed pause. Assessment is of fictional learning. Any optional personal reflection stays with the pupil and is not collected, photographed, displayed or compared.
marking: Retain actual fictional work and the first response. Record usual access separately from adult content prompts. Give one NS and allow an actual reply in the learner's own colour or usual mode. E only for actual saved evidence. R only after Voice, Audience, one NS and the actual pupil response. Offer to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm mapping.
assessment: This is the assessing week. The six-outcome tick-and-comment grid starts blank. Record actual evidence, work reference, context, usual access and content prompts. Use observed, more learning needed or not observed honestly; pass is not observed. Relevant earlier actual work may inform a judgement, with its reference. One task does not prove every outcome or lasting behaviour. The grid is not an award checklist. Staff check the actual requirements and sufficiency before offering evidence for the unit award. No automatic bank or award is claimed.
outcomes: Recognise emotions and healthy ways to manage stress.
Build personal resilience and a growth mindset.
Understand mental health and where to get support.
Stay safe online; recognise risks and my digital footprint (Safer Internet Day).
Know how to report concerns and seek help.
